name: snap (pure-Rust Snappy)
baseline: Snappy C++ 1.1.8 through the same benchmark harness
verdict_reason: The claim is parity, and the table shows it: per-file results land within about 10% of C++ in both directions, with snap ahead on text decompression and behind on pdf decompression. It is a pure-Rust drop-in, not a speedup.
tier_reason: First-party table from a public harness with the CPU named, but no rustc version or flags stated.
claimed_speedup: Parity with C++ Snappy: decompress txt2 1001.8 vs 916.6 MB/sec (1.09x faster), txt4 930.2 vs 857.2 MB/sec; compress gaviota 602.3 vs 563.5 MB/sec; but decompress pdf 15.3 vs 16.8 GB/sec (1.10x slower) and compress urls 542.0 vs 566.3 MB/sec.
workload: Snappy's own microbenchmark corpus (html, urls, jpg, pdf, text, protobuf files), raw block compress and decompress.
platforms: Any Rust target; parity measured on x86_64
one_liner: Pure-Rust Snappy with raw and frame formats; measured within about 10% of C++ Snappy either way on x86_64.
how_it_is_fast: A close port of the C++ algorithm with unaligned word loads and copies, plus a hand-written frame format. It matches C++ rather than beating it.
use_it_when: You need Snappy without a C++ toolchain
You need the Snappy frame format, which the C++ binding crate lacks
skip_it_when: You are looking for a speedup over the C++ library; there is none to find
caveats: Run in 2020 against Snappy 1.1.8 on an Intel i7-6900K (2016); no newer comparison published
No rustc version or flags stated
tradeoffs: Snappy itself trades ratio for speed, and LZ4 decoders beat it in lz4_flex's benchmark; pick snap for Snappy compatibility, not speed

evidence.quote: The performance of this implementation should roughly match the performance of the C++ implementation on x86_64.
These benchmarks were run with Snappy/C++ 1.1.8.
Benchmarks were run on an Intel i7-6900K.
